questions.stem: What causes the components of a mixture to separate in chromatography?
options: Differences in the masses of the components, so heavier ones are pulled down by gravity
Differences in how quickly each component reacts chemically with the mobile phase
Differences in how strongly each component interacts with the stationary and mobile phases
Differences in the colours of the components, which absorb different amounts of light
questions.explanation: Each component is shared between the stationary phase and the moving mobile phase. One that is attracted more strongly to the stationary phase moves more slowly, so the components separate. No chemical reaction takes place.

questions.stem: In thin layer chromatography, how is the Rf value of a spot calculated?
options: Distance moved by the spot ÷ total length of the plate
Time taken by the spot ÷ time taken by the solvent front
Distance moved by the spot ÷ distance moved by the solvent front
Distance moved by the solvent front ÷ distance moved by the spot
questions.explanation: Rf compares how far the spot travels with how far the solvent travels, both measured from the starting line, so it is always between 0 and 1. Inverting the ratio would give values greater than 1.

questions.stem: On a TLC plate, a spot has moved 3.0 cm from the starting line and the solvent front has moved 7.5 cm. What is the Rf value?
questions.explanation: Rf = 3.0 / 7.5 = 0.40. Dividing the other way gives 2.5, which is impossible because a spot cannot travel further than the solvent.

questions.stem: A TLC plate coated with polar silica is developed with a non-polar solvent. Which component of a mixture travels furthest?
options: The component with the largest mass
The component present in greatest amount
The least polar component
The most polar component
questions.explanation: Polar components are attracted strongly to the polar silica and move slowly. The least polar component is attracted least to the stationary phase and most to the non-polar mobile phase, so it travels furthest.

questions.stem: On a silica (polar) TLC plate, compound A has an Rf of 0.80 and compound B an Rf of 0.20. Which statement is correct?
options: B is more soluble in the solvent, so it moves more slowly
A has a larger molar mass, so it moves further up the plate
B is more polar, so it is held more strongly by the silica
A is more polar, so it is held more strongly by the silica
questions.explanation: A low Rf means the compound spent more time attached to the stationary phase. On polar silica, the compound held most strongly is the more polar one, so the more polar compound is B. Greater solubility in the solvent would make a compound move faster, not slower.

questions.stem: A sample sold as a single pure substance gives three spots on a TLC plate. What can be concluded?
options: The sample has reacted with the solvent to form three spots
The sample contains at least three different substances
The sample contains exactly one substance in three forms
The sample is pure, because each spot has a different Rf
questions.explanation: Each spot is a component that travels at its own rate, so three spots show at least three substances. There may be more, because two substances can have the same Rf in a given solvent.

questions.stem: How can a component of a mixture be identified using TLC?
options: Compare its Rf with known standards run on the same plate under the same conditions
Measure the height of the solvent front, which is different for every substance
Compare the size of its spot with spots of known substances on a different plate
Measure the time it takes to reach the top, which is the same in any solvent
questions.explanation: Rf values depend on the stationary phase, solvent and temperature, so the most reliable comparison is with standards run alongside the sample. A matching Rf suggests, but does not prove, the same substance.

questions.stem: In TLC, why must the sample spots be placed above the level of the solvent in the tank?
options: Otherwise the spots would be too heavy and sink to the bottom of the tank
Otherwise they would dissolve into the solvent pool instead of travelling up the plate
Otherwise the solvent would react with the spots and change their colours completely
Otherwise the solvent front could not rise at all, as the spots would block it
questions.explanation: If the spots were below the solvent surface, the sample would wash off into the solvent in the tank. Above it, the solvent rises past them by capillary action and carries the components up the plate.

questions.stem: In gas chromatography, what is the mobile phase?
options: A thin layer of silica coated on a glass plate
A polar liquid coated on the inside of the column
An unreactive carrier gas such as nitrogen or helium
A liquid solvent pumped through at high pressure
questions.explanation: In GC an inert gas carries the vaporised sample through a long column. The liquid or solid coating inside the column is the stationary phase, and a liquid pumped at high pressure is the mobile phase in HPLC.

questions.stem: In gas or high performance liquid chromatography, what is the retention time of a component?
options: The time from injecting the sample until that component reaches the detector
The time the sample takes to vaporise after it is injected into the instrument
The time from the first component reaching the detector until the last one does
The time a component stays at the detector before the next component arrives
questions.explanation: Retention time is measured from injection to detection. Under fixed conditions it is characteristic of a substance, so it can be compared with standards to identify components.

questions.stem: Hexane (boiling point 69 °C) and octane (boiling point 126 °C) are separated by gas chromatography on a non-polar column. Which has the shorter retention time, and why?
options: Octane, because its larger molecules are pushed through faster by the gas
Hexane, because it is more volatile and spends more time in the carrier gas
Octane, because it is more volatile and spends more time in the carrier gas
Hexane, because it is attracted more strongly to the non-polar stationary phase
questions.explanation: Both are non-polar, but octane has stronger dispersion forces, a higher boiling point and a stronger attraction to the stationary phase. Hexane is more volatile, spends more time in the moving gas, and reaches the detector first.

questions.stem: A gas chromatogram of a mixture of two compounds shows two peaks. Peak X has 30% of the total peak area and peak Y has 70%. What can be concluded, if the detector responds equally to both?
options: Compound Y has a longer retention time than compound X
Compound X is more volatile than compound Y in the column
The mixture contains equal amounts of compounds X and Y
The mixture contains more of compound Y than compound X
questions.explanation: Peak area is proportional to the amount of each component reaching the detector, so Y makes up the larger share. Peak area says nothing about retention time or volatility, which come from the position of the peak.

questions.stem: Which chromatographic technique is best suited to analysing a non-volatile drug that decomposes when heated?
options: Gas chromatography at high temperature
Gas chromatography with helium gas
Fractional distillation of the sample
High performance liquid chromatography
questions.explanation: HPLC uses a liquid mobile phase at room temperature, so the sample does not need to be vaporised. Gas chromatography requires the sample to be vaporised, which would decompose a heat-sensitive drug.

questions.stem: Which technique is best suited to detecting very small amounts of volatile organic pollutants in a sample of air?
options: Gas chromatography
Thin layer chromatography
Paper chromatography
Flame testing
questions.explanation: Gas chromatography separates volatile compounds and its detectors are very sensitive, so it can find tiny amounts of pollutants in air. TLC and paper chromatography need larger samples and are less sensitive, and flame tests identify metal ions.

questions.stem: An HPLC column has a non-polar stationary phase, and the mobile phase is a polar mixture of water and methanol. Which component of a mixture reaches the detector first?
options: The component with the most carbon atoms
The component present in the smallest amount
The most polar component
The least polar component
questions.explanation: With a non-polar stationary phase, non-polar components are held back while polar components stay in the polar mobile phase and move through quickly. This is the reverse of TLC on polar silica.

questions.stem: HPLC standards of caffeine give peak areas of 200 for 10 ppm and 400 for 20 ppm. A drink sample, run under the same conditions, gives a caffeine peak area of 300. What is its caffeine concentration?
options: 15 ppm
30 ppm
1.5 ppm
20 ppm
questions.explanation: Peak area is proportional to concentration: 20 area units per ppm. An area of 300 corresponds to 300 / 20 = 15 ppm. Reading the area of 300 as 30 ppm ignores the calibration.

questions.stem: In gas chromatography, what happens to the retention times of the components if the column temperature is increased?
options: They become longer, as the stationary phase holds hot molecules more strongly
They become shorter, as the components spend more time in the gas phase
They become longer, as the carrier gas moves more slowly when it is hot
They stay the same, as retention time depends only on the substance
questions.explanation: At a higher temperature, components are more volatile and spend a greater share of time in the moving carrier gas, so they pass through faster. This is why retention times are only compared under identical conditions.

questions.stem: Why is chromatography widely used in drug testing of athletes' urine samples?
options: It measures the pH of the urine, which changes when banned drugs are present in it
It identifies drugs by the colour of the flame they produce when they are burnt
It can separate and identify tiny amounts of many substances in a small, complex sample
It changes the drugs into harmless substances, so the sample can be safely discarded
questions.explanation: Urine is a complex mixture. GC and HPLC can separate its components and, by comparing retention times with standards, detect very small amounts of a banned substance. Chromatography is a physical separation, not a chemical change.

questions.stem: Which statement is part of the Kinetic Theory of an ideal gas?
options: The particles lose energy in each collision, so they gradually slow down
The average kinetic energy of the particles is proportional to the absolute temperature
The particles attract each other strongly, which keeps the gas inside its container
The particles take up most of the volume of the container that the gas is in
questions.explanation: In the model, ideal gas particles are in constant random motion, have negligible volume, exert no attractive forces and collide elastically. Their average kinetic energy is proportional to the temperature in kelvin.

questions.stem: According to the Kinetic Theory, what causes the pressure of a gas?
options: Gas particles reacting with the walls of the container
Gas particles colliding with the walls of the container
Gas particles attracting each other across the container
Gas particles expanding in size as they are heated up
questions.explanation: Pressure is the force per unit area from countless collisions of fast-moving particles with the walls. Particles do not grow in size when heated; they move faster.

questions.stem: The volume of a fixed amount of gas is halved at constant temperature. What happens to the pressure, and why?
options: It doubles, because particles hit the walls twice as often
It halves, because there is less space for particles to move
It doubles, because the particles now move twice as fast
It stays the same, because the temperature has not changed
questions.explanation: In half the volume, the same particles at the same average speed strike each part of the wall twice as often, so the pressure doubles. The particles' speed depends on temperature, which has not changed.

questions.stem: A sealed balloon is placed in a freezer and shrinks. Which explanation is correct?
options: The particles shrink in the cold, so the gas inside takes up a smaller volume overall
The cold makes some gas particles leak out through the balloon, so the volume falls
The particles stop moving at freezer temperatures, so they settle at the bottom
The particles slow down and hit the walls less often and less hard, so the balloon contracts
questions.explanation: Cooling lowers the average kinetic energy of the particles. Their collisions with the inside of the balloon become less frequent and less forceful, so the balloon contracts until the pressure inside again balances the pressure outside. The particles themselves do not shrink.

questions.stem: A sealed aerosol can carries the warning 'Do not heat'. According to the Kinetic Theory, why could heating make the can burst?
options: The particles attract each other more strongly when heated, pulling the can apart
The particles move faster and hit the walls harder and more often, so the pressure rises
The particles become larger when heated, so they need more room than the can provides
The heat causes more gas particles to form by splitting, so there are more collisions
questions.explanation: The can is rigid, so its volume cannot change. Heating raises the particles' kinetic energy, so they collide with the walls more often and with more force, and the pressure may exceed what the can can withstand.

questions.stem: Which change increases the pressure of a fixed amount of gas?
options: Decreasing its volume at constant temperature
Increasing its volume at constant temperature
Cooling it at constant volume
Removing some of the gas at constant volume
questions.explanation: Squeezing the same particles into a smaller space increases the frequency of collisions with the walls. Expanding, cooling or removing gas all make collisions with the walls less frequent or less forceful.

questions.stem: Under which conditions does a real gas behave least like an ideal gas?
options: Low pressure and high temperature
Low pressure and low temperature
High pressure and high temperature
High pressure and low temperature
questions.explanation: At high pressure the particles are close, so their own volume matters, and at low temperature they move slowly, so attractive forces between them become significant. Both break the assumptions of the ideal gas model.

questions.stem: Two sealed flasks, each of 1.0 L, are at the same temperature and pressure. One contains hydrogen and the other carbon dioxide. What do the two samples have in common?
options: The same density of gas
The same number of atoms
The same number of molecules
The same mass of gas
questions.explanation: Equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of particles, which is why one mole of any ideal gas has the same molar volume. CO₂ molecules are heavier and contain three atoms each, so mass, density and atom count differ.

questions.stem: Taking the molar volume at STP as 22.71 L mol⁻¹, what volume does 0.500 mol of nitrogen gas occupy at STP?
questions.explanation: V = n × Vm = 0.500 × 22.71 = 11.4 L. The molar volume is the same for any ideal gas at STP, so the identity of the gas does not matter.

questions.stem: Taking the molar volume at STP as 22.71 L mol⁻¹, how many moles of oxygen are in 4.54 L of the gas at STP?
options: 5.00 mol
103 mol
questions.explanation: n = V / Vm = 4.54 / 22.71 = 0.200 mol. Multiplying the volume by the molar volume gives 103, which is far too large.

questions.stem: 10.0 g of calcium carbonate (M = 100.09 g mol⁻¹) reacts with excess hydrochloric acid: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. Taking the molar volume at STP as 22.71 L mol⁻¹, what volume of CO₂ forms at STP?
questions.explanation: n(CaCO₃) = 10.0 / 100.09 = 0.0999 mol, and the mole ratio CaCO₃ : CO₂ is 1 : 1, so V = 0.0999 × 22.71 = 2.27 L. Using the 2 of the HCl coefficient instead gives 4.54 L.

questions.stem: Magnesium reacts with excess acid: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. Taking the molar volume at STP as 22.71 L mol⁻¹, what mass of magnesium (M = 24.31 g mol⁻¹) produces 1.00 L of hydrogen at STP?
questions.explanation: n(H₂) = 1.00 / 22.71 = 0.0440 mol. The ratio Mg : H₂ is 1 : 1, so n(Mg) = 0.0440 mol and m = 0.0440 × 24.31 = 1.07 g. The value 0.0440 is the amount in moles.

questions.stem: Carbon monoxide burns: 2CO(g) + O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g). What volume of oxygen reacts with 10.0 L of carbon monoxide, both measured at the same temperature and pressure?
questions.explanation: At the same temperature and pressure, gas volumes are in the same ratio as moles. CO : O₂ is 2 : 1, so 10.0 L of CO needs 5.0 L of O₂.

questions.stem: For a dilute solution in water, a concentration of 1 ppm is equal to approximately:
options: 1 mg of solute per litre of solution
1 g of solute per litre of solution
1 mol of solute per million litres
1 µg of solute per litre of solution
questions.explanation: Parts per million is 1 mg of solute per kg of solution. A litre of a dilute aqueous solution has a mass of about 1 kg, so 1 ppm is about 1 mg L⁻¹. 1 g L⁻¹ would be 1000 ppm.

questions.stem: A town water supply contains 0.025 g of fluoride ions in every 25 L. What is the fluoride concentration in ppm?
options: 25 ppm
1000 ppm
1.0 ppm
questions.explanation: 0.025 g = 25 mg, and 25 mg / 25 L = 1.0 mg L⁻¹, which is 1.0 ppm. Leaving the mass in grams gives 0.0010, which is the concentration in g L⁻¹, not ppm.

questions.stem: What is the concentration in g L⁻¹ of a solution made by dissolving 5.0 g of glucose in water to give 250 mL of solution?
options: 5.0 g L⁻¹
20 g L⁻¹
questions.explanation: 250 mL = 0.250 L, so c = 5.0 / 0.250 = 20 g L⁻¹. Multiplying by 0.250 instead of dividing gives 1.25.

questions.stem: What is the concentration in g L⁻¹ of a 0.250 mol L⁻¹ sodium chloride solution (M = 58.44 g mol⁻¹)?
options: 234 g L⁻¹
questions.explanation: Each litre holds 0.250 mol, which has a mass of 0.250 × 58.44 = 14.6 g, so the concentration is 14.6 g L⁻¹. Dividing the molar mass by the concentration gives 234.

questions.stem: A guideline limit for a heavy metal in drinking water is 0.010 ppm. A 500 mL sample of bore water contains 0.0080 mg of the metal. Which statement is correct?
options: It exceeds the limit, with a concentration of 0.016 ppm
It is within the limit, with a concentration of 0.0080 ppm
It is within the limit, with a concentration of 0.0040 ppm
It exceeds the limit, with a concentration of 16 ppm
questions.explanation: Concentration = 0.0080 mg / 0.500 L = 0.016 mg L⁻¹ = 0.016 ppm, which is above 0.010 ppm. Using the mass without converting to a litre gives 0.0080, and multiplying by 0.500 gives 0.0040.

questions.stem: A sample of hard water contains 40 ppm of calcium ions. Use Ca = 40.08. What is the calcium ion concentration in mol L⁻¹?
options: 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ mol L⁻¹
1.6 × 10³ mol L⁻¹
1.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹
1.0 mol L⁻¹
questions.explanation: 40 ppm is about 40 mg L⁻¹, or 0.040 g L⁻¹. Dividing by the molar mass gives 0.040 / 40.08 = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹. Forgetting to convert milligrams to grams gives 1.0 mol L⁻¹.
